short: Decoder split (M06) and lip-reader text plus audio prompt (M07) are standard; WER gain comes from the lip reader, LRS3 WER level with LipVoicer, prosody leads confounded by the prompt.
position: RESOUND [@pham2025resound] changes the decoder (M06), splitting it into excitation and formant paths, and the use-time inputs (M07), adding lip-reader text and a 0.5 s audio prompt. Both are standard: source-filter synthesis from silent video dates to Vid2Speech [@ephrat2017vid2speech] and pitch and energy predictors to Let There Be Sound [@kim2024let], so the claim to be "the first study to incorporate source-filter theory into L2S synthesis" (§1; Appendix, M06) holds only as a label. The intelligibility gain comes from the lip reader: without L2T and SRA, LRS3 WER rises from 20.06 to 27.49, level with Intelligible L2S at 27.69 (Tables 1, 3). With it, RESOUND matches the field's best: 20.06 against 21.04 for LipVoicer in its table and 21.4% in LipVoicer's paper [@yemini2024lipvoicer], and 28.55 against 17.04 on LRS2. The prosody and similarity leads (MAEF0 49.52 against 81.63, SECS 0.777 against 0.591 for LipVoicer) pit a system prompted with audio (§3.3) against systems given none. The SOTA claim (§5) rests on no reported repeated runs and baseline rows of unstated provenance.
